title: Diabetic retinopathy detection from fundus photographs
summary: A two-track image classification competition — build a CNN from scratch, and fine-tune a pretrained one. Best models scored 0.780 and 0.826 AUC.
context: Private Codabench competition run as coursework (MSc); no public leaderboard to link to

sections.heading: The problem
body: Detecting diabetic retinopathy from retinal photographs. The original labels are a 0-4 clinical severity scale, collapsed to binary for the competition, which left a 73/27 class split. There were 2,000 training images, 500 validation, 1,000 test, split across two separate tracks — one where you train a CNN from scratch, one where you fine-tune an ImageNet backbone. With only 2,000 training images, overfitting was the constant risk on both sides.

sections.heading: Approach
body: Both tracks shared a preprocessing pipeline: unify image orientation, crop to the retinal disc, and apply Ben Graham contrast normalisation. I handled the class imbalance twice over, with a weighted loss and a weighted sampler.

Two decisions came from the medical problem itself rather than from tuning. Microaneurysms are the main signal for early retinopathy and they're small, so on the fine-tuning track I worked at 380px instead of the usual 224. And fundus cameras don't have a fixed orientation, so rotating only ±15 degrees throws away most of the valid rotations — using the full ±180 range worked a lot better.

The from-scratch track ended up as a 5-block CNN, about 1M parameters, averaged over three seeds. The fine-tuning track was a weighted ensemble of DenseNet121, DenseNet169 and ResNeXt50, unfrozen in two stages, with the ensemble weights chosen by grid search on validation. Both used 4-pass test-time augmentation.

sections.heading: Result
body: 0.826 AUC on the private test set for the fine-tuning track, 0.780 for the from-scratch one.

The interesting part was what didn't work, and there was a lot of it. CLAHE broke the crop step because it changed the global intensity the cropping depended on. A dtype bug in the contrast normalisation caused pixel overflow and turned every image grey — that sent us backwards below our own first baseline until I found it. Adding SE blocks and residual connections to the custom model overfit immediately. The aggressive ±180 augmentation that helped the pretrained models failed completely from scratch, at 0.53 AUC. And unfreezing a third DenseNet block overfit, so two stages was the right place to stop.

I also dropped a fourth backbone (SE-ResNeXt50) from the final ensemble even though it scored fine on its own, because its predictions correlated too closely with ResNeXt50 and it wasn't adding anything.
